## 5 Crazy Roman Emperors
Some stories might make you giggle… but the ancient Romans under their rule sure weren’t laughing.
Indeed, just a quick note to take a pause for thought:Many of the stories about Rome’s most “outrageous” emperors come from ancient historians like Suetonius, Tacitus, and Cassius Dio.
While their writings are invaluable, they were often influenced by political bias, hearsay, and a taste for scandal. In other words, some of these tales may be exaggerated—or even invented—making it important to separate historical fact from ancient gossip.
So, without futher ado, here is a list of **the famous five crazy Roman emperors.**

## **Tiberius**
### When he ruled
14-37 AD

## **Tiberius**
### **Why he was crazy**
The **ultimate “dirty old man,”** Tiberius succeeded Augustus, Rome’s first emperor, only to soon withdraw into his elaborate villa in Capri. Suetonius, the first-century historian, tells us that his life there was **nothing short of depraved:**
*   Ancient sources claim that Tiberius indulged in shocking behavior on Capri, but modern historians debate how much of this was exaggerated for effect. Apparently he **hired young boys and girls** to frolic like “Pans and nymphs” in the grottoes, and kept an erotic library “in case a performer should need an illustration of what was required”.
**Truth-o-meter (0=completely false, 10=definitely true):**
*   6. **Suetonius loved scandals,** but he’s a more believable source than some other historians, like Tacitus, and he’s telling us rumors that were actually **very popular** in Tiberius’ time.  
*   While Tiberius may not have been quite as depraved as Suetonius makes him out to be, it’s safe to say you wouldn’t have sent your children to go hang out with Uncle Tiberius for the summer.

## **Tiberius**
### **Where to find out more about Tiberius**
Few bits of classical history are juicier than Suetonius’s _Life of Tiberius_(in his _Lives of the Caesars),_ which **goes into way more graphic detail** than we’ve written. For those who are really fascinated, the first 6 books of Tacitus’s _Annals_ are **dedicated to Tiberius’ reign,** although modern historians are a bit more skeptical of his accounts.
In Italy, you can get closer to Tiberius (if you dare) at the Palatine Hill, which still has the **ruins of his palace,** or at Capri, where you can see the Villa Jovis, **one of his 12 villas on the island.**

## Caligula: The emperor who declared war on the sea
### When he ruled
37-41 AD

## Caligula: The emperor who declared war on the sea
### **Why he was crazy**
**Everyone loved Caligula** when he became emperor, seeing him as the **youthful, fresh face** to follow Tiberius. Unfortunately, it quickly became apparent that Caligula was **also a delusional megalomaniac**and like Tiberius, he too was considered as one of the crazy Roman emperors.
He **wandered the palace throughout the night** instead of sleeping, flew into public rages, and spoke to the moon and to Jupiter as if they were in confidence. In the best-known story, he **made his horse a senator,** building it a stable of marble and inviting people to have dinner with the horse.
**Truth-o-meter:**
*   8. Most of what we know about Caligula comes from Suetonius, who **wrote 80 years after his death,** or Cassius Dio, who wrote **more than 100 years after _that._**Still, almost every source about him, including contemporary ones, **characterizes Caligula as insane.**  
*   One **main source is, again, Suetonius,** whose description of Caligula makes it sound like he **suffered from a psychotic illness** – not too surprising, and something that would have been exacerbated by how everyone else around him had to participate in his delusions at pain of death.

## Caligula: The emperor who declared war on the sea
### Where to find out more about Caligula
Again, Suetonius’s _Life of Caligula_ in the _Lives of the Caesars_ is a good bet. There’s also Cassius Dio’s _Roman History_ and the 6th book of Tacitus’ _Annals._
Caligula was also the **force behind many public works,** and the remains of **one of the most important,** the Claudian Aqueduct, can be seen near the Caelian and Palatine Hills in central Rome, or in the Parco degli Acquedotti. His other aqueduct, the**Acqua Anio Novus**, remains part of the Aurelian Wall.

## **Tiberius**
### **Why he was crazy**
The **ultimate “dirty old man,”** Tiberius succeeded Augustus, Rome’s first emperor, only to soon withdraw into his elaborate villa in Capri. Suetonius, the first-century historian, tells us that his life there was **nothing short of depraved:**
*   Ancient sources claim that Tiberius indulged in shocking behavior on Capri, but modern historians debate how much of this was exaggerated for effect. Apparently he **hired young boys and girls** to frolic like “Pans and nymphs” in the grottoes, and kept an erotic library “in case a performer should need an illustration of what was required”.
**Truth-o-meter (0=completely false, 10=definitely true):**
*   6. **Suetonius loved scandals,** but he’s a more believable source than some other historians, like Tacitus, and he’s telling us rumors that were actually **very popular** in Tiberius’ time.  
*   While Tiberius may not have been quite as depraved as Suetonius makes him out to be, it’s safe to say you wouldn’t have sent your children to go hang out with Uncle Tiberius for the summer.

## **Tiberius**
### **Where to find out more about Tiberius**
Few bits of classical history are juicier than Suetonius’s _Life of Tiberius_(in his _Lives of the Caesars),_ which **goes into way more graphic detail** than we’ve written. For those who are really fascinated, the first 6 books of Tacitus’s _Annals_ are **dedicated to Tiberius’ reign,** although modern historians are a bit more skeptical of his accounts.
In Italy, you can get closer to Tiberius (if you dare) at the Palatine Hill, which still has the **ruins of his palace,** or at Capri, where you can see the Villa Jovis, **one of his 12 villas on the island.**

## Caligula: The emperor who declared war on the sea
### **Why he was crazy**
**Everyone loved Caligula** when he became emperor, seeing him as the **youthful, fresh face** to follow Tiberius. Unfortunately, it quickly became apparent that Caligula was **also a delusional megalomaniac**and like Tiberius, he too was considered as one of the crazy Roman emperors.
He **wandered the palace throughout the night** instead of sleeping, flew into public rages, and spoke to the moon and to Jupiter as if they were in confidence. In the best-known story, he **made his horse a senator,** building it a stable of marble and inviting people to have dinner with the horse.
**Truth-o-meter:**
*   8. Most of what we know about Caligula comes from Suetonius, who **wrote 80 years after his death,** or Cassius Dio, who wrote **more than 100 years after _that._**Still, almost every source about him, including contemporary ones, **characterizes Caligula as insane.**  
*   One **main source is, again, Suetonius,** whose description of Caligula makes it sound like he **suffered from a psychotic illness** – not too surprising, and something that would have been exacerbated by how everyone else around him had to participate in his delusions at pain of death.

### Where to find out more about Caligula
Again, Suetonius’s _Life of Caligula_ in the _Lives of the Caesars_ is a good bet. There’s also Cassius Dio’s _Roman History_ and the 6th book of Tacitus’ _Annals._
Caligula was also the **force behind many public works,** and the remains of **one of the most important,** the Claudian Aqueduct, can be seen near the Caelian and Palatine Hills in central Rome, or in the Parco degli Acquedotti. His other aqueduct, the**Acqua Anio Novus**, remains part of the Aurelian Wall.

**Gaius Julius Caesar Augustus Germanicus** (31 August AD 12 – 24 January AD 41), also called **Gaius** or **Caligula** (), was the third Roman emperor, ruling from AD 37 until his assassination in AD 41. He was the son of the Roman general Germanicus and Agrippina the Elder, Augustus's granddaughter, members of the first ruling family of the Roman Empire. He was born two years before Tiberius became emperor. Gaius accompanied his father, mother and siblings on campaign in Germania, at little more than four or five years old. He had been named after Gaius Julius Caesar, but his father's soldiers affectionately nicknamed him "Caligula" ('little boot').[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caligula#cite_note-3)
texts.1:
Germanicus died in Antioch in AD 19, and Agrippina returned with her six children to Rome, where she became entangled in a bitter feud with Emperor Tiberius, who was Germanicus' biological uncle and adoptive father. The conflict eventually led to the destruction of her family, with Caligula as the sole male survivor. In 26, Tiberius withdrew from public life to the island of Capri, and in 31, Caligula joined him there. Tiberius died in 37, and Caligula succeeded him as emperor, at the age of 24.
Of the few surviving sources about Caligula and his four-year reign, most were written by members of the nobility and Senate, long after the events they purport to describe. For the early part of his reign, he is said to have been "good, generous, fair and community-spirited",[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caligula#cite_note-4) but increasingly self-indulgent, cruel, sadistic, extravagant, and sexually perverted thereafter, an insane, murderous tyrant who demanded and received worship as a living god, humiliated the Senate, and planned to make his horse, Incitatus, a consul. Most modern commentaries instead seek to explain Caligula's position, personality and historical context. Some historians dismiss many of the allegations against him as misunderstandings, exaggeration, mockery or malicious fantasy.
texts.2: During his brief reign, Caligula worked to increase the unconstrained personal power of the emperor, as opposed to countervailing powers within the principate. He directed much of his attention to ambitious construction projects and public works to benefit Rome's ordinary citizens, including racetracks, theatres, amphitheatres, and improvements to roads and ports. He began the construction of two aqueducts in Rome: the Aqua Claudia and the Anio Novus. During his reign, the empire annexed the client kingdom of Mauretania as a province. He had to abandon an attempted invasion of Britain, and the installation of his statue in the Temple in Jerusalem. In early 41, Caligula was assassinated as a result of a conspiracy by officers of the Praetorian Guard, senators, and courtiers. At least some of the conspirators might have planned this as an opportunity to restore the Roman Republic and aristocratic privileges. If so, their plan was thwarted by the Praetorians, who seem to have spontaneously chosen Caligula's uncle Claudius as the next emperor. Caligula's death marked the official end of the Julii Caesares in the male line, though the Julio-Claudian dynasty continued to rule until the demise of Caligula's nephew, the Emperor Nero.
texts.3: Caligula was born in Antium on 31 August AD 12, the third of six surviving children of Germanicus and his wife and second cousin, Agrippina the Elder. Germanicus was a grandson of Mark Antony, and Agrippina was the daughter of Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa and Julia the Elder, making her the granddaughter of Augustus.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caligula#cite_note-FOOTNOTESuet._''Calig.''7-5) The future emperor Claudius was Caligula's paternal uncle.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caligula#cite_note-FOOTNOTECassius_Dio59.6-6) Caligula had two older brothers, Nero and Drusus, and three younger sisters, Agrippina the Younger, Julia Drusilla and Julia Livilla.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caligula#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarrett201520%E2%80%9321-7)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caligula#cite_note-FOOTNOTESuet._''Calig.''7-5) At the age of two or three, he accompanied his father, Germanicus, on campaigns in the north of Germania.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caligula#cite_note-FOOTNOTESuet._''Calig.''9-8) He wore a miniature soldier's outfit devised by his mother to please the troops, including army boots (_caligae_) and armour.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caligula#cite_note-FOOTNOTESuet._''Calig.''9-8) The soldiers nicknamed him _Caligula_ ("little boot"). Winterling believes he would have enjoyed the attention of the soldiers, to whom he was something of a mascot, though he later grew to dislike the nickname.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caligula#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWinterling201119%E2%80%9320-9)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caligula#cite_note-10)
texts.4: Germanicus was a respected, immensely popular figure among his troops and Roman civilians of every class, and was widely expected to eventually succeed his uncle Tiberius as emperor.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caligula#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWinterling201119%E2%80%9321-11) For his successful northern campaigns, he was awarded the great honour of a triumph. During the triumphal procession through Rome, Caligula and his siblings shared their father's chariot, and the applause of the populace. A few months later, Germanicus was despatched to tour Rome's allies and provinces with his family. They were received with great honour; at Assos Caligula gave a public speech, aged only 6. Somewhere _en route_, Germanicus contracted what proved to be a fatal illness. He lingered awhile, and died at Antioch, Syria, in AD 19, aged 33, convinced that he had been poisoned by the provincial governor, Gnaius Calpurnius Piso.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caligula#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarrett201530-12)[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caligula#cite_note-13) Many believed that he had been killed at the behest of Tiberius, as a potential rival.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caligula#cite_note-FOOTNOTESuet._''Calig.''2-14)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caligula#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWinterling201121%E2%80%9324-15)
texts.8: Winterling observes that a forthright protest would "certainly have cost him his life".[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caligula#cite_note-FOOTNOTESuet._''Calig.''10-16)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caligula#cite_note-FOOTNOTETacitus[[s:The_Annals_(Tacitus)/Book_6#20|VI.20]]-28)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caligula#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWinterling201138%E2%80%9343-29)
texts.9: In 33, Caligula's mother and his brother Drusus died, while still in exile.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caligula#cite_note-FOOTNOTETacitus[[s:The_Annals_(Tacitus)/Book_6#23|6.23%E2%80%9325]]-30) In the same year, Tiberius arranged the marriage of Caligula and Junia Claudilla, daughter of one of Tiberius' most influential allies in the Senate, Marcus Junius Silanus. Caligula was given an honorary quaestorship in the _\_cursus honorum\__, a series of political promotions that could lead to consulship. He would hold this very junior senatorial post until his sudden nomination as emperor.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caligula#cite_note-FOOTNOTECassius_Dio[httpspenelopeuchicagoeduThayerERomanTextsCassius_Dio58html23_LVII.23]-31) Junia died in childbirth the following year, along with her baby.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caligula#cite_note-FOOTNOTESuet._''Calig.''12-24) In 35, Tiberius named Caligula as joint heir with Tiberius' grandson, Gemellus,[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caligula#cite_note-FOOTNOTESuet._''Calig.''76-32) who was Caligula's junior by seven years and not yet an adult. At the time, Tiberius seemed to be in good health, and likely to survive until Gemellus' majority.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caligula#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarrett201551%E2%80%9353-33)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caligula#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWinterling201149%E2%80%9351-34)
texts.10: In Philo's account, Tiberius was genuinely fond of Gemellus, but doubted his personal capacity to rule and feared for his safety should Caligula come to power. Suetonius claims that Tiberius, ever mistrustful but still shrewd in his mid-70s, saw through Caligula's apparent self-possession to an underlying "erratic and unreliable" temperament, not one to be trusted in government; and he claims that Caligula took pleasure in cruelty, torture, and sexual vice of every kind. Tiberius is said to have indulged the young man's appetite for theatre, dance and singing, in the hope that this would help soften his otherwise savage nature; "he used to say now and then that to allow Gaius to live would prove the ruin of himself and of all men, and that he was rearing a viper for the Roman people and a Phaethon for the world."[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caligula#cite_note-FOOTNOTESuet._''Calig.''11-35) Winterling points out that this judgment draws on later, not particularly accurate accounts of Caligula's rule; Suetonius credits Tiberius with a knowledge of human nature which in reality was not only foreign to him, but famously unsound. At Capri, Caligula learned to dissimulate. He probably owed his life to that and, as all the ancient sources agree, to Macro.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caligula#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWinterling201148-36)[[c]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caligula#cite_note-37) Many believed, or claimed to believe, that given a little more time, Tiberius would have eliminated Caligula as a possible successor, but died before this could be done.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caligula#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWinterling201149%E2%80%9351-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caligula#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarrett201550%E2%80%9352-38)

Tiberius died on 16 March AD 37, a day before the Liberalia festival. He was 77 years old. Suetonius, Tacitus, and Cassius Dio repeat variously elaborated rumours which held that Caligula, perhaps with Macro, was directly responsible for his death.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caligula#cite_note-FOOTNOTESuet._''Calig.''12-24)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caligula#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWiedemann1996221-39)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caligula#cite_note-FOOTNOTETacitus[[wikisource:The_Annals_(Tacitus)/Book_12#53|XII.53]]-40)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caligula#cite_note-FOOTNOTECassius_Dio[httpspenelopeuchicagoeduThayerERomanTextsCassius_Dio58html_lviii._28]-41)Philo and Josephus, the latter a Romano-Jewish writer who served Vespasian a generation later, describe Tiberius' death as natural.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caligula#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPhilo''On_the_Embassy''_[[s:On_the_Embassy_to_Gaius#IV|IV.25]]-42)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caligula#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJosephusXIII.6.9-43) On the same day, Caligula was hailed as emperor by members of the Praetorian guard at Misenum. His leadership of the _domus Caesaris_ ("Caesar's household") as its sole heir and pater familias was ratified by the senate, who acclaimed him _imperator_ two days after the death of Tiberius.
texts.12: Caligula entered Rome on 28 or 29 March, and with the consensus of "the three orders" (senate, equestrians and common citizens) the Senate conferred on him the "right and power to decide on all affairs".[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caligula#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWinterling201150%E2%80%9351-44)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caligula#cite_note-:3-45) Caligula was the first emperor to acquire all of his powers at once rather than over the course of his reign like Augustus and Tiberius.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caligula#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBowmanGarnseyRathbone200812-46)

## Civil and military career
### Tiberius in Capri, with Sejanus in Rome
The affair of Sejanus and the final years of treason trials permanently damaged Tiberius's image and reputation. After Sejanus's fall, Tiberius's withdrawal from Rome was complete; the empire continued to run under the inertia of the bureaucracy established by Augustus, rather than through the leadership of the _Princeps_. Suetonius records that he became paranoid,[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiberius#cite_note-FOOTNOTESuetonius,_''Tiberius''60,_62%E2%80%9364-91) and spent a great deal of time brooding over the death of his son. During this period there was a short invasion by Parthia, and incursions on Roman territories by Dacian and Germanic tribes.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiberius#cite_note-FOOTNOTESuetonius,_''Tiberius''41-93)
Little was done to plan or secure Tiberius's succession. The Julians and their supporters were diminished in numbers and political influence, thanks to Sejanus, and Tiberius's immediate heirs were dead. Caligula, the sole surviving son of Germanicus, or Tiberius's own grandson, Tiberius Gemellus, were possibly candidates.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiberius#cite_note-FOOTNOTETacitus,_''Annales''[[s:The_Annals_(Tacitus)/Book_6#46|VI.46]]-94) However, Tiberius only made a half-hearted attempt at the end of his life to make Caligula a quaestor, and thus give him some credibility as a possible successor, while Gemellus himself was still only a teenager and thus completely unsuitable for some years to come.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiberius#cite_note-FOOTNOTECassius_Dio[httpspenelopeuchicagoeduThayerERomanTextsCassius_Dio57html23_LVII.23]-95)

## Civil and military career

Tiberius died in Misenum on 16 March AD 37, months before his 78th birthday.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiberius#cite_note-96)[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiberius#cite_note-FOOTNOTETacitus,_''Annales''[[s:The_Annals_(Tacitus)/Book_6#50|VI.50%E2%80%9351]]-97) While ancient sources agree on the date and location of his death, contradictory accounts exist of the precise circumstances.
Tacitus relates that the emperor appeared to have stopped breathing, and that Caligula, who was at Tiberius's villa, was being congratulated on his succession to the empire, when news arrived that the emperor had revived and was recovering his faculties. He goes on to report that those who had moments before recognised Caligula as Augustus fled in fear of the emperor's wrath, while Macro took advantage of the chaos to have Tiberius smothered with his own bedclothes.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiberius#cite_note-FOOTNOTETacitus,_''Annales''[[s:The_Annals_(Tacitus)/Book_6#50|VI.50%E2%80%9351]]-97)
Suetonius reports that, upon recovering after an illness, and finding himself deserted by his attendants, Tiberius attempted to rise from his couch, but fell dead. Suetonius further reports several rumours, including that the emperor had been poisoned by Caligula, starved, and smothered with a pillow.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiberius#cite_note-FOOTNOTESuetonius,_''Tiberius''73-98)Seneca the Elder also reports Tiberius having died a natural death.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiberius#cite_note-macsphere_mcmaster_ca-99)

## Civil and military career
### Tiberius in Capri, with Sejanus in Rome
According to Cassius Dio, Caligula, fearing that the emperor would recover, refused Tiberius's requests for food, insisting that he needed warmth, not food; then, assisted by Macro, he smothered the emperor in his bedclothes.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiberius#cite_note-FOOTNOTECassius_Dio[httpspenelopeuchicagoeduThayerERomanTextsCassius_Dio58html_lviii._28]-100)[[d]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiberius#cite_note-101)[[e]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiberius#cite_note-103) Neither Josephus, Pliny, nor Philo relate the story of Tiberius's suffocation, stating simply the date of his death and/or the length of his reign._[citation needed_]
After his death, the Senate refused to vote Tiberius the divine honours that had been paid to Augustus, and mobs filled the streets yelling "To the Tiber with Tiberius!" (the bodies of criminals were typically thrown into the river, instead of being buried or burnt).[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiberius#cite_note-104) However, the emperor was cremated, and his ashes were placed in the Mausoleum of Augustus.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiberius#cite_note-105)
In his will, Tiberius nominated Caligula and Tiberius Gemellus as his joint heirs.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiberius#cite_note-FOOTNOTESuetonius,_''Tiberius''76-106) Caligula's first act on becoming _Princeps_ was to void Tiberius's will.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiberius#cite_note-FOOTNOTECassius_Dio[httpspenelopeuchicagoeduThayerERomanTextsCassius_Dio59html1_LIX.1]-107)
